title: Low-cost mechanical storage with high efficiency over long periods

concept.text: The proposed innovation is mechanical energy storage that combines low cost, useful scale, long service life, and high efficiency after extended storage, while substantially expanding where economical systems can be installed. Mechanical storage holds energy in physical states such as rotation, raised masses, or compressed fluids, then converts it back into useful output. The breakthrough target is a demonstrated combination of performance and deployment advantages; perfect efficiency and zero loss over years are unnecessary.

As an engineering synthesis, the central distinction is between an effective storage component and an effective complete installation. A system must retain energy during the waiting period, charge and discharge efficiently, and limit the electricity consumed by supporting equipment. It must also provide useful capacity and power at an acceptable site, with affordable construction, containment, maintenance, and replacement. Improvements in one component would qualify only if they produce a substantial advantage at the system level.

significance.text: Conditionally, achieving this combination could make storage economical for applications currently constrained by installation cost, location, storage duration, or standby consumption. Affordable capacity that remains useful after long waiting periods could allow energy to be shifted across longer supply gaps, while durability could reduce replacement requirements. These are consequences of the proposed capability, not demonstrated benefits of a system identified in the supplied evidence.

The potentially revolutionary change would be a large expansion in accessible, economically useful mechanical storage. The research identifies pumped storage and flywheels as existing approaches, so the innovation does not depend on treating mechanical storage itself as new. Its importance would depend on how much a demonstrated system improves on contemporary alternatives for particular applications.

As a downstream possibility, better storage could support greater use of variable electricity generation and improve flexibility in some power systems. It would not alone establish a fully renewable grid, remove transmission and integration requirements, or guarantee superiority to batteries. Applications value power, duration, efficiency, location, and response differently; a transformative advantage in one setting need not transfer to all others.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability, as defined by this proposal, is a complete mechanical storage installation that simultaneously delivers economical capacity, useful power, durability, high efficiency over long holding periods, and materially broader deployment options. The supplied record does not establish through a current cross-technology comparison whether this combination remains unmet in every relevant application. The open target should therefore be evaluated against named use cases and contemporary alternatives.

As an engineering synthesis, the barriers differ by storage mechanism. Siting and civil works can constrain gravity-based installations; pressure or rotor containment can impose structural and safety requirements; limited energy density can increase space or material needs. Conversion equipment can dominate cost, while friction, aerodynamic drag, leakage, and supporting equipment can reduce delivered energy. These are candidate constraints to investigate for a selected design, rather than a verified comparative assessment of every mechanical storage family.

The research attributes a narrower example to Amiryar and Pullen: their flywheel model examines how bearing and windage losses affect standby and system performance. This illustrates why efficient charging and discharging alone do not establish efficient long-duration storage. However, the supplied review had no retained article text with which to verify the model assumptions or findings, and the attribution should not be generalized to all flywheels or all mechanical storage.

current_state.text: The supplied research describes several mechanical storage forms as already practical and frames the frontier as expanding their economical deployment. The accompanying review could not verify that broad characterization from inspectable source material. The record therefore provides background context, but no independently inspectable deployment inventory, current performance comparison, or demonstration of the proposed breakthrough.

The sole indexed publication is Mustafa E. Amiryar and Keith R. Pullen’s “Analysis of Standby Losses and Charging Cycles in Flywheel Energy Storage Systems,” dated 27 August 2020 in the supplied research. That research attributes to Sections 4–5 an analysis of bearing and aerodynamic losses and their effects on standby and round-trip performance in a modeled flywheel design. This is a design-specific modeling attribution, not a reported demonstration of inexpensive mechanical storage retaining high efficiency over multiple weeks.

The source index marks the article as not captured and contains no retained artifacts. The review consequently could not independently check its contents, modeling assumptions, or the magnitude of the reported effects. No numerical efficiency, retention, or cost values are available in the supplied material for responsible inclusion here. This evidence limitation does not show that the paper’s findings are false.

No documented freshness search was supplied to establish the field’s status as of 1 November 2026. Accordingly, neither present-day openness of the proposed capability nor a current cross-technology cost benchmark can be established from this record. The dated flywheel analysis also does not establish that the proposed system-level combination is achievable.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a grid-connected mechanical storage installation, or one at comparably relevant scale and operating conditions, for a clearly named application. Independently measure charging energy, usable discharged energy, capacity, power, and performance over both daily and multiweek holding periods. Repeat the operating cycles sufficiently to characterize consistency and emerging degradation. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurement boundaries: report charging and discharging losses, energy retained during storage, and auxiliary consumption separately, alongside an explicitly defined overall round-trip efficiency. Specify whether supporting equipment draws power from the stored energy or an external supply, and include that consumption in the complete energy accounting. Report operating conditions, measurement uncertainty, and changes in usable capacity so that a favorable conversion-efficiency figure cannot obscure poor retention or substantial standby demand.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed measurement boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic test: choose a contemporaneous, application-matched baseline before testing and define the cost and efficiency improvements that would count as substantial. Distinguish installed capital cost from lifecycle cost, and disclose assumptions about utilization, maintenance, replacement, service life, and energy losses. A credible claim of lower lifecycle cost should show how measured performance supports the calculation and how uncertain assumptions affect the result.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed economic test

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: make the operating protocol, energy accounting, uncertainty analysis, and sufficient design information available for independent assessment and repeat testing. Report containment requirements, footprint, site dependence, maintenance, and degradation. Tests across multiple holding times and operating conditions would establish the breadth actually demonstrated; they would not establish universal superiority across sites, storage mechanisms, or grid applications.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: MEC-02, “Service-life superlubricity in ordinary machine contacts,” and MEC-12, “Predictive mechanics of real, evolving surface contacts,” overlap with the management of friction and contact losses in storage machinery. MEC-11, “Transferable prediction of wear and component life,” overlaps with maintenance planning and reliable lifecycle estimates. These concepts address contact behavior and component longevity; MEC-14 requires a favorable complete storage system even if those component advances become available.

MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” and MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” could conditionally improve repeatedly loaded structures, rotors, or containment. Their targets concern material capabilities. Stronger or more fatigue-resistant components would not by themselves establish economical storage, low standby consumption, or broad siting flexibility.

MEC-01, “An engineering-predictive theory of turbulent flow,” could overlap with predicting aerodynamic or fluid losses where those effects matter. MEC-03, “Engines that make sub-100 °C heat worth converting,” has a more conditional connection through thermal management or recovery of low-temperature heat in suitable system designs. Neither concept is equivalent to storing mechanical energy efficiently over long periods, and neither is established here as a prerequisite.

MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” overlaps with designing machinery that meets multiple constraints. MEC-14 is narrower in application and more demanding in measured operational and economic outcomes: producing a feasible mechanism does not establish a competitive storage installation. These roster relationships are conceptual synthesis, not evidence of demonstrated dependencies between the innovations.

change_log.change: Preserved MEC-14’s identity as a system-level mechanical storage breakthrough and expanded the explanation of complete-installation performance.
change_log.reason: The research and review agree that the target is a useful combination of capabilities, rather than perfect efficiency or the invention of mechanical storage.

change_log.change: Qualified broad statements about existing deployments, cross-technology constraints, and the capability remaining missing.
change_log.reason: The supplied review lacked inspectable evidence for those comparisons and a documented freshness search.

change_log.change: Retained the dated flywheel modeling attribution while explicitly stating its design-specific scope and missing source artifacts.
change_log.reason: The attribution supplies useful technical context, but the review could not verify the article contents or generalize its findings.

change_log.change: Separated conversion losses, storage retention, auxiliary consumption, and overall round-trip efficiency in the proposed evaluation.
change_log.reason: The review identified these measurement distinctions as necessary to interpret long-duration performance.

change_log.change: Distinguished installed capital cost from lifecycle cost and required an application-matched baseline chosen before testing.
change_log.reason: Economic significance depends on comparable service requirements and disclosed lifetime assumptions.

change_log.change: Integrated conditional impact, reproducibility, practical limits, and relevant roster distinctions into their respective sections.
change_log.reason: These preserve the review’s scientific reasoning without treating hypothetical benefits or proposed tests as achieved results.

unresolved_issues: The indexed 2020 article has no retained text or artifacts, leaving its detailed assumptions and findings unverified within the supplied record.
No current cross-technology evidence establishes which applications already meet parts or all of the proposed capability.
The target application, storage mechanism, capacity, power, holding period, and acceptable site requirements remain unspecified.
Numerical cost, efficiency, retention, durability, and improvement thresholds remain to be chosen against an application-matched baseline; none can be established from the supplied evidence.
No demonstrated installation or independently reproduced result in the supplied material establishes that the full proposed combination is achievable.
